summary: In 2012, NASA’s VIIRS instrument began replacing MODIS for fire tracking. The result? Earlier years now look about five times quieter than they really were. That false jump makes it hard to tell whether any season is truly unusual, and it is the gap Pyronac closes. It estimates what VIIRS would have reported for those years, creating one consistent record from 2003 on. On unseen years, typical monthly error fell from about 78% to about 9%. With that record in place, dispatchers, crew leads, and land managers can pick an area and years to get a hot-spot calendar, an anomaly map and a CSV download. A base planner builds on it too, suggesting fire base sites to study: sites chosen from 2003 to 2015 reached 67% of later fires near towns, versus 23% for random sites.
details:
What it does. A dispatcher, crew lead or land manager picks an area on a globe and a range of years. Pyronac draws a calendar of fire activity: a row per year since 2003, a column per month, darker where more fire was detected. A Raw/Harmonized switch shows the false jump after 2012, then removes it. A panel compares any month with the usual for that month in other years, a map shows where it was unusual, and the data downloads as CSV.

How it works. A hot spot is one satellite pixel where fire was detected. MODIS, the older instrument, has pixels about 1 km across; VIIRS has 375 m pixels, so it sees smaller fires and reports several times more. Pyronac counts hot spots per month in squares about 11 km across. For months before February 2012 it estimates what VIIRS would have reported: a machine learning model for Canada, a measured ratio per region and month for India and Brazil. When Suomi NPP, the satellite that sets the scale, stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026, the record continued on NOAA-20, with the same instrument.

Proof. The method learned from 2012 to 2019 and was tested on 2020 to 2025, years it never saw, when both instruments were flying, so each estimate can be checked against what VIIRS really reported. A typical monthly total was about 78% off for raw MODIS and about 9% off harmonized, across three countries.

Benefits and impact. Land managers get one record of two decades, not two that cannot be compared. Dispatchers and crews see whether a month is unusual for that place and season. The long view changes: in the southern Amazon the raw record shows fire rising 48% a decade; harmonized, it is falling 36%.

The base planner. The planner suggests candidate sites for small fire bases in Canada. Each site has a reach, a planning distance of 100 km, and goes where it brings most summer fire near towns within reach. It tests itself: 25 sites chosen from 2003 to 2015 alone reached 67% of the fire near towns in 2016 to 2025; random sites, 23%. Harmonizing does not move the sites. It changes how much fire to plan for: in the raw record, Canada's years before 2012 look 4.6 times quieter. These are sites to study: the record knows where fire was, not roads, water or land cover.

What makes it creative. Each country uses whichever method did better on years it never saw, by a rule fixed before the test. When the satellite that sets the scale stopped delivering data, the record carried on. Every estimated month shows its likely range. The planner grades itself on years it never saw.

Factors we considered. Validity: against Canada's reported area burned, the estimates before 2012 may be 15 to 21% low, and Canada's monthly totals are the least exact of the three. Limits: the planner covers Canada, June to August, and towns of 500 or more, so small villages are missing; positions are good to about 11 km; some sit in prairie farm country, where most hot spots are crop burning. Hard questions: fire renews the boreal forest, and agencies monitor some fires that threaten no community, so only fire near towns counts; burned forest has less fuel, so sites are tested on later years. Accessibility: colour scales readable with colour vision deficiency, a number behind every colour, keyboard use.

Built with. Python, DuckDB, scikit-learn, FastAPI, TypeScript, React, MapLibre GL JS. Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m; NASA Black Marble base map; GeoNames towns.
